w: Carl Milles filled his own garden with his own sculptures, then left the lot to the public when he died in 1955. Terraces climb the cliffside above the water on Lidingo, statues posed against open sky rather than gallery walls -- the artist's home turned into his own best exhibition.
s: A sculptor's clifftop garden of his own work
_facts: Art museum and sculpture garden on the island of Lidingö in Stockholm
Former home of sculptor Carl Milles (1875-1955) and his wife Olga Milles (1874-1967)
Consists of the artists' former home, an art gallery, and a sculpture park

w: The world's biggest spherical building represents the Sun in the Sweden Solar System -- the planets are scattered across the country at the same scale, some hundreds of kilometres off. Renamed for Avicii after the DJ's death, locals still call it Globen, and so does the metro station underneath.
s: The Sun in a scale model of the solar system
_facts: Originally Stockholm Globe Arena, then Ericsson Globe, now Avicii Arena; still called Globen locally
Indoor arena in Stockholm Globe City, Johanneshov district
Represents the Sun in the Sweden Solar System, the world's largest scale model of the Solar System
The local metro station is still named Globen metro station

w: Every book, pamphlet and recording ever published in Swedish is supposed to end up here by law, alongside anything published abroad with a Swedish connection -- a complete paper trail of a language and a country's arguments with itself, quietly filed away and preserved for good.
s: The legal deposit copy of an entire language
_facts: Kungliga biblioteket (KB), Sweden's national library
Collects and preserves all domestic printed and audio-visual materials in Swedish
Also collects Swedish-association content published abroad; major foreign-language research collections

w: Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz spent decades turning a former gravel pit into a cemetery where pine forest, meadow and stone do the work usually left to headstones. Opened in 1920, it tracks their own style shifting from classicism to functionalism -- and UNESCO listed the whole thing in 1994.
s: A gravel pit turned UNESCO-listed cemetery
_facts: The Woodland Cemetery, in the Gamla Enskede district south of central Stockholm
Inaugurated 1920; UNESCO World Heritage List 1994
Designed by Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz; reflects a shift from Nordic Classicism to functionalism

w: Torben Grut's brick stadium hosted the 1912 Olympics -- athletics, wrestling, tug of war and the running leg of the modern pentathlon all inside its narrow oval. More than a century on it still holds around 14,000 for sport, the same brick towers still framing the track underneath.
_facts: Designed by Torben Grut, opened 1912 as the main venue for the 1912 Olympic Games
Hosted athletics, equestrian, football, gymnastics, the pentathlon's running leg, tug of war and wrestling
Capacity of 13,145-14,500 depending on usage, up to almost 33,000 for concerts

w: Artur Hazelius moved whole farmhouses, a church and a manor house onto this hill in 1891 to preserve a Sweden he thought industrialisation was about to erase. It worked almost too well: 'skansen' became the generic word for open-air museums everywhere from Wisconsin to Eastern Europe.
s: The original open-air museum, copied worldwide
_facts: Oldest open-air museum and zoo in Sweden, on the island of Djurgården
Opened 11 October 1891 by Artur Hazelius to show pre-industrial Swedish ways of life
The term 'skansen' became a generic name for open-air museums elsewhere, e.g. Old World Wisconsin

w: The Swedish crown has held rights over this island since the 1400s, and technically still does -- the Royal Court's own administration runs it today. What was once a royal hunting ground is now the city's favourite green lung, its forests and meadows drawing some ten million visitors a year.
s: A royal hunting ground since the 1400s
_facts: Officially Kungliga Djurgården, 'the Royal Animal Park', an island in central Stockholm
Since the 15th century the Swedish monarch has owned or held rights of disposition, now via the Royal Djurgården Administration
Part of the National City Park since 1995; attracts over ten million visitors a year

w: Every December the Blue Hall here fills with tuxedos and gowns for the Nobel Prize banquet, then goes back to being a municipal office building the rest of the year. It sits right on the water at the tip of Kungsholmen, and its tower can be climbed for the view the banquet guests never get to see.
s: Where the Nobel Prize banquet is held
_facts: Stockholms stadshus, seat of Stockholm Municipality on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen island
Houses offices, conference rooms and ceremonial halls
Venue of the Nobel Prize banquet; one of Stockholm's major tourist attractions

w: Built as a Greyfriars monastery church in the Middle Ages, this is where most Swedish monarchs have ended up for burial ever since -- a plain brick shell outside, a room full of royal sarcophagi within. The monks are long gone; the kings and queens stayed.
s: The burial church of Sweden's monarchs
_facts: Riddarholmskyrkan, church of the former medieval Greyfriars Monastery
Final resting place of most Swedish monarchs
